name: Hafted stone-tipped javelins in the Middle Stone Age Ethiopian Rift
summary: Middle Stone Age people in the Ethiopian Rift fixed obsidian points to shafts to make javelins more than 279,000 years ago.
description: Sahle and colleagues interpret pointed obsidian artifacts from the Gademotta Formation in the Main Ethiopian Rift as early composite projectile points. The specimen context is more than 279,000 years old.

impact.note: Hafted points became common across Middle Stone Age Africa (reach 2) and a head on a shaft was a new kind of tool (depth 2), but descent of later hafting from this population, as opposed to earlier or separate origins, is unproven, so reach is not put at 3 and generativity is held at 1, in line with the spear-thrower record.

date.label: more than 279,000 years ago (before c. 277,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Sahle and colleagues interpreted pointed obsidian artifacts from the Gademotta Formation as projectile points. The earliest context studied is older than 279,000 years.

evidence.supports: used as projectile weapons (in the form of hafted javelin tips) as early as >279,000 years ago
Separate geochemical study of a broad formation sample found most pieces match Worja obsidian. This result concerns assemblage provenance.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Kathu Pan 1 (about 500,000 years) needs checking against Wilkins and colleagues (2012) and the critiques; if it holds it would be a separate, earlier southern African record, which is what the lead asked for.
Hafting at Gademotta is inferred from fracture and damage analysis, not shown by residues or surviving hafts.
Gademotta coordinates were entered from memory (the ridge west of Lake Ziway) and not taken from a fetched source.
The relation to Neanderthal birch-tar hafting in Europe (dataset record birch-bark-tar-for-stone-tool-backing) is not addressed by the source.

research.note: The source reports the earliest stone-tipped projectiles but also cites an older, disputed claim of hafted spears at Kathu Pan, and it does not say whether hafting at Gademotta arose there or was inherited from earlier populations.

caveats: The identification is an inference from archaeological artifact analysis. Separate geological analysis assigns most of a broader Gademotta obsidian sample to nearby Worja, with some other or uncertain assignments. Geological provenance alone does not establish the function or individual source of each point.
